processing: Depends on the region: lightly oxidised, ball-rolled and unroasted for high-mountain tea; moderately oxidised and roasted for Dong Ding and Hong Shui; strip-shaped and barely oxidised for Wenshan Bao Zhong. The better grades are always hand-picked.
harvest_season: Spring and winter in the mountains (the two prized pickings), with summer and autumn harvests added at lower elevations; the bush sprouts later and recovers more slowly than Jin Xuan or Si Ji Chun.
appearance_dry: Small, tightly rolled dark-green balls (or slender twisted strips in the Bao Zhong style) with a short pale stem, typically smaller and denser than Jin Xuan.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green when green-processed, gold to amber when roasted, always bright and clear.
appearance_wet: Small, oval, thick leaves with a fine serrated edge, dark green with a thin red rim in the green styles and brown-edged in roasted ones.
taste_profile: A clean orchid-and-lily fragrance, a sweet and slightly oily body, a gentle citrus-peel brightness and a cooling finish that keeps returning; roasting turns the florals into honey, ripe fruit and toasted grain.

brewing.notes: Water at or just off the boil in every style; the cultivar is more forgiving of heat than of cool water, which makes it thin and grassy. Lengthen the first steep for rolled leaf, shorten it for Bao Zhong.

vintage_note: You rarely buy 'Qing Xin' as such: it is sold under the regional name (Alishan, Li Shan, Dong Ding, Bao Zhong) by season, spring and winter of the current year for the mountains and year-round from the lowlands, and the cultivar name on the packet is mainly a quality signal because cheaper Jin Xuan and Si Ji Chun are often passed off under the same regional names. Green styles are drunk within a year; roasted Qing Xin keeps for years and is the leaf most Taiwanese aged oolong is made from.
description:
Qing Xin oolong, the 'green heart' cultivar, is the bush behind most of the Taiwanese oolongs people fall in love with: Dong Ding, the high-mountain teas of Alishan, Shan Lin Xi and Li Shan, and Wenshan Bao Zhong are all, in their best versions, made from it. Growers also call it Ruan Zhi, 'soft stem', and old farmers simply 'zhong zai'; Taiwanese growers have also planted it in northern Thailand and the Vietnamese highlands, which is where a lot of cheap 'Taiwanese oolong' actually comes from.

It is thought to have arrived from Fujian in the 1800s, and it is a difficult plant: low-yielding, slow to recover after picking, prone to disease and fussy about soil, which is exactly why the Tea Research and Extension Station spent decades breeding higher-yielding alternatives such as Jin Xuan and Cui Yu. Farmers keep planting it anyway because nothing else gives the same aroma and the same long, cool aftertaste. The leaves are small, oval and dark, the bush stays low, and at altitude it grows slowly and makes thick, sweet leaf.

What the cultivar itself brings to the cup, before region and roast get a say, is a clean orchid-and-lily fragrance, a sweet, slightly oily body, a gentle citrus-peel brightness and a finish that cools the throat and keeps returning. Processed green and rolled it is all florals and cream; oxidised and roasted it turns to honey, ripe fruit and toasted grain; made as strip-shaped Bao Zhong it is the lightest and most perfumed. Brew it with water at or just off the boil in all of those styles; it is more forgiving of heat than of cold water.

You rarely buy 'Qing Xin' as such. It is sold under the regional name, by season, and the cultivar name on the packet is mostly a quality signal, because the cheaper Jin Xuan and Si Ji Chun are often passed off under the same regional names. Ask; a good seller will tell you which cultivar is in the bag.

Do not confuse it with its namesakes: Qing Xin Da Mou is a different bush, grown for Oriental Beauty, and Qing Xin Gan Zai is the small-leaf cultivar behind Sanxia's green teas.
sources_note: The Fujian origin in the 1800s is the usual account but not documented precisely; 'zhong zai' as a farmers' nickname is from memory.
